checklist_comments: Calm, overcast, mild temps. We started on the golf course where we were quickly escorted off, then checked creek and lower section. We finally found a (restricted) birding agreement for covering this place. Exotics (annoyingly) persists, though (luckily) the species don't seem to have yet taken hold in ensenada. Very happy to finally encounter two true vagrants here on the same visit, plus quite a few very good birds that were not traditional vagrants!----Day notes: On this day, we encountered the most incredible wave of Eastern passerine vagrants I have personally ever experienced in Baja. The combination of overcast, light winds (the ideal weather for the Baja north coast but seemingly not farther south), and incredible reports from San Diego and offshore Baja had us all excited for the prospects of today--and it panned out! There were vagrants EVERYWHERE! Not only a great introduction to Baja for CWH and AWH, but started the motto of "I've never seen anything here" leading to a vagrant that held through the entire trip.

checklist_comments: Strong NW winds, clear. We spent a while here seawatching and trying to find a way out to Natividad, but that ended up flat. Luckily the seawatching was extremely productive, by far the most lucrative watch I've ever had here. Dick posited the possibility of our high success with Storm-Petrels having some correlation with a delayed effect of the Hurricane, which could well be an explanation (Storm-Petrels are normally not visible from here, or at least in anywhere near these kinds of numbers). ----"it's a really good sign how long they've been gone"----Day notes: This visit set the tone and pace for the remainder of the trip. After a poor visit to tortugas, the true highlight of the day was seawatching at Eugenia. We spent much of the morning trying to figure out if there was a way to get onto natividad, which we ultimately concluded was truly closed for COVID (we'll have to try again next Fall). The traps heading back to the mainland, as well traps off of the peninsula in the ensuing days, were very dead.

checklist_comments: In March 23 and April 3, 2000, I participated in a West Virginia University Field Ornithology class that traveled through the Baja Peninsula. The class was led by Dr. Robert C. Whitmore, Division of Forestry, Wildlife and Fisheries Science and Management. We arrived at 1:40 PM in Cabos San Lucas and traveled to Centro de Investigaciones Biológicas del Noroeste among other locations. Dr. Whitmore was studying Brown thrashers and Yellow "Mangrove" warblers, in particular. These records are recorded from a detailed field notebook that included maps, sketches, descriptions, and other notes. There were approximately 10 to 12 students on this trip and although we observed species as a group, we oftentimes were dispersed in groups of two. Mist-netting and song playback were used at some locations. Temperature and weather were mid 80s and breezy, cooling into late afternoon and evening. This was a memorable trip and contributed toward my curiosity and admiration of desert ecosystems, rural lifestyles, and global surf culture. The people were kind and interesting. The food was fantastic. The heat was real. The desert and coast were magnificent. Oh yes... and the birds!

Two juvenile birds near the landing cove.  In the field I assumed Black-crowned but on photo review the structure of the bird was a bit off for Black-crowned. Initially had difficulty discerning which species I was looking at when I reviewed pictures. They were showing small triangular spots on the back and wings with thin white lines but to me this was not the best field mark but was a contributing factor. The spots were sharper looking than the blurry triangular spots on Black-crowned. These birds on Anacapa have a heavier looking bill and more blunt tip than expected on Black-crowned which is also rare for this location. Consulted more experience birders and they confirmed Yellow-crowned Night Heron.  At least one of the birds was standing tall and seemed to have long legs, and a thinner body with a more blocky head. To me Black-crowned seem stockier with a more rounded head into a thicker neck.

checklist_comments: 55-64 degrees, sunny with 50% cloud cover, light breeze 3mph. Rose and I started in the Goleta Beach Park parking lot east of Sandspit Rd. and observed the southern side of the Goleta water channel. We drove to the parking lot west of Sandspit and took the paved path at the north side of the lot, across the wooden Rock Pigeon bridge and back. We walked on the bike path east and crossed Sandspit bridge and continued northeast. After the narrow 217 bike path bridge, we took the muddy dirt trail along the north side of the Atascadero Creek until just shy of Ward Dr. We headed north to the bike trail and walked west and south on the bike trail, eventually returning to our car. Our first time birding this location (we weren't sure how most birders cover this area and meandered a bit - it was fun). Later, I realized that we covered two hotspots plus non-hotspot territory, but I didn't break up the list while birding and the mileage was low. I changed the hotspot to Atascadero Creek Trail since more species were seen at this location vs. Goleta Slough areas A & H. Track mileage: 2.568.

I did not see a bent toe on this bird, but my views of the feet were brief (while walking or scratching the body) as they were mostly out of view as the bird perched in bulrushes. Like the bird at the marina, this is a second-year bird and is molting in the the bold black head pattern. The back feathers were gray with pale edges, the primaries and secondaries appeared gray, the tertials still seemed to show some brown and gray tones (light dependent), and the wing coverts were brown.
